title: Can Trust in Science Be Improved? An Adaptive Experiment Testing Student-Designed Messages
summary: Can short, student-designed messages raise trust in science? We ran a registered online survey experiment with US adults recruited through Lucid. Respondents were randomly assigned to a pure control or to one of 32 messages (videos, images, text, news stories and a values exercise), and trust in science was measured afterwards. Of 11,519 raw respondents, 8,572 passed the screener and 7,803 entered the models. Message 2 (video) lowered trust in science by 0.171 scale points (95% CI [−0.262, −0.080], p = 0.0002) relative to a control mean of 3.685. Message 26 (video) also lowered it, by 0.104 points (95% CI [−0.184, −0.024], p = 0.010). Three videos, Messages 12, 15 and 20, showed small positive effects of about 0.06 points (p < 0.05). Other arms were not distinguishable from control. Becaus

extensions.label: Generalizability
extensions.why: Addresses the missing moderator and sample causes: the one nominal Republican interaction (Message 15, +0.165, p = 0.004) was found across 32 tests and needs a targeted confirmatory test.
extensions.title: Partisan and platform boundary of the video effects
extensions.hypothesis: Message 15 raises trust more among Republicans than non-Republicans (interaction about +0.165). Effects are smaller in the feed than under forced exposure.
extensions.primary_outcome: Trust in science: mean of 6 items, with items 4-6 reverse-coded (post_science_1 to post_science_6).

extensions.label: Theoretical debate
extensions.why: Fixes the multiplicity and power problem: a preregistered confirmatory test of 4 arms replaces 32 exploratory contrasts, so the two positions of the debate are discriminated.
extensions.title: Replicate the extremes to separate real effects from chance
extensions.hypothesis: If brief messages can move trust, Messages 15 and 20 will raise post-trust by about +0.06 and Message 2 will lower it by -0.10 or more. If the original hits were chance, all four contrasts will shrink toward zero.
extensions.primary_outcome: Post-treatment trust in science: mean of six items, with items 4-6 reverse-coded.

potential.verdict: A follow-up is worth running, but as a narrow confirmation rather than another broad screen. Only Message 2's backlash is clearly distinguishable from noise, and the three small gains of about 0.06 points are at the level expected from 32 uncorrected tests. Run the replication of the extreme arms first, since it is cheap and resolves whether any of the gains is real. Then, if the gains replicate, run the format-by-content factorial with a delayed wave to learn about mechanism and persistence. The retrieved literature is thin on this question, so the debate is framed from the study's own question plus two loosely related works.
